Dolphins are regarded as the friendliest creatures in the sea and stories of them helping drowning sailors have been common since Roman times. The more we learn about dolphins, the more we realize that their society is more complex than people previously imagined. They look after other dolphins when they are ill, care for pregnant mothers and protect the weakest in the community, as we do. Some scientists have suggested that dolphins have a language but it is much more probable that they communicate with each other without needing words. Could any of these mammals be more intelligent than man? Certainly the most common argument in favour of man's superiority over them that we can kill them more easily than they can kill us is the least satisfactory. On the contrary, the more we discover about these remarkable creatures, the less we appear superior when we destroy them.
It is clear from the passage that dolphins

  1. don't want to be with us as much as we want to be with them
  2. are proven to be less intelligent than once thought
  3. have a reputation for being friendly to humans
  4. are the most powerful creatures that live in the oceans

Suppose that the system uses preemptive, round-robin scheduling and that $\text{T}_{11}$ is running when the quantum expires.
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline
\text{Process} & \text{Threads within the process} \\\hline
\text{P}_1 & \text{T}_{11}, \text{T}_{12} \\
\text{P}_2 & \text{T}_{21}, \text{T}_{22} \\
\text{P}_3 & \text{T}_{31}\\\hline
\end{array}$$

  1. $\text{T}_{12}$
  2. $\text{T}_{21}$
  3. $\text{T}_{22}$
  4. $\text{T}_{31}$

Consider the following program segment:

if A > B then

else
    if B > C then
        V[i] := G(i)

Assume that the values of the Boolean expressions $\text{“A > B”}$  and $\text{“B > C”}$ are independent and that, on the average, $\mathrm{A}>\mathrm{B}, 75$ percent of the time and $\text{B > C}, 25$ percent of the time.   2. $\text{F} : 7,500, \mathrm{G} : 625$
  3. $\text{F} : 7,500, \mathrm{G} : 1,875$
  4. $\text{F} : 7,500, \mathrm{G}: 2,500$

The page table is moved to the main memory and accessed via a TLB. Each main memory access takes $50$ ns and each TLB access takes $10$ ns. Each virtual memory access involves:

  • if TLB miss: mapping VPN to PPN using page map in main memory $(50$ ns)
  • accessing main memory at appropriate physical address $(50$ ns)

  1. $0.98$
  2. $0.95$
  3. $0.96$
  4. $0.90$

\begin{array}{ll}
\text{F} \rightarrow . \text{L} & \{\text { F.v }=\mathrm{L} . \mathrm{v}\} \\

& \text { L.v } \left.=\text{L}_1 \cdot \mathrm{v}+2^{-\text{L} . l} \cdot \mathrm{B} . \mathrm{v}\right\} \\
\text{L} \rightarrow \text{B} & \{\text { L.l=1 }, \mathrm{L} \cdot \mathrm{v}=\mathrm{B} . \mathrm{v} / 2\} \\

$$

An integer array $\text{A}$ is $\boldsymbol{k}$-even-mixed if there are exactly $k$ even integers in $\text{A}$, and the odd integers in $\text{A}$ appear in sorted order. Given a $k$-even-mixed array $\text{A}$ containing $n$ distinct integers for $k=\lceil n / \lg n\rceil$, Let $O\left(n^a(\log n)^b\right)$ be tightest bound to sort $\text{A}.$ What will be the values of $\text{a}$ and $b$?

What will be the tightest bound on the worst-case time complexity of the following function $\textsf{sun()}?$

void sun(int n) {
    int k = 0;
    for(int i = 1; i < n; i *= 2) {
        k++;
    }
    for(int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if(k % 5 == 0) {
            k--;
        }
        else {
            for(int j = 0; j < k; j++) {
                printf("let's go to the beach");
            }
        }
    }
}
  1. $\text{O}(n \log n)$
  2. $\text{O}(\log n)$
  3. $\text{O}\left(n^ 2\right)$
  4. $\text{O}\left(n^ 3\right)$

Codd's rule of physical data independence is that

  1. all information in the database is to be represented in one and only one way, namely by values in column positions within rows of tables.
  2. all views that are theoretically updatable must be updatable by the system.
  3. changes that are made to the physical storage representations or access methods must not require changes be made to application programs.
  4. changes that are made to tables that do not modify any of the data already stored in the tables must not require changes be made to application programs.

  2. $\text{P}_1$’s requests will always be satisfied without even checking if resulting state (after processing $\text{P}_1$’s requests) is in safe state or not.
  3. Processes requests will always be satisfied in the same order as safe state sequence and we can not satisfy any out of order process request.
  4. We can never satisfy any request coming from $\text{P}_n$ without satisfying request from $\mathrm{P}_1$.

$\mathrm{B}^+$-trees have different structures for leaf and non-leaf nodes.
In $\mathrm{B}^+$- tree leaf node contains keys and record pointer associated with it and a block pointer pointing to the next leaf node. Non-leaf nodes contains only keys and child pointer, there is no need to store record pointer at non-leaf node, because all keys are ultimately present on leaf node. For leaf node order will be maximum number of keys, record pointer pair a node can hold, but order of non leaf node is determined by maximum child pointers it can have.

Assume that all student names are of length 8 bytes, disk blocks are of size 512 bytes, and index pointers, record pointers are of size $4$ bytes, $5$ bytes respectively. Given this scenario, the best choice for the order of leaf node and non-leaf node is $\mathrm{X}, \mathrm{Y}$ respectively. Then what is $\mathrm{Y}-\mathrm{X}$ ?

Two more exotic relational algebra operators are the semijoin $(\ltimes)$ and antijoin $(\triangleright)$. Semijoin is the same as natural join, except only attributes of the first relation are returned in the result. For example, if we have relations $\textsf{Student(ID, name)}$ and $\textsf{Enrolled(ID, course)},$ and not all students are enrolled in courses, then the query "Student $\ltimes$ Enrolled" returns the ID and name of all students who are enrolled in at least one course. In the general case, $\text{E}_1 \ltimes \text{E}_2$ returns all tuples in the result of expression $\text{E}_1$ such that there is at least one tuple in the result of $\mathrm{E}_2$ with matching values for the shared attributes. antijoin is the converse: $\text{E}_1 \triangleright \text{E}_2$ returns all tuples in the result of expression $\text{E}_1$ such that there are no tuples in the result of $\text{E}_2$ with matching values for the shared attributes. For example, the query "Student $\triangleright$ Enrolled" returns the ID and name of all students who are not enrolled in any courses.
